# Which compute changes: question selection, shorter generation, branching, or conditional replay?

[简体中文](../../../../learning/deep-dives/post-training/data-and-budget.md) · English

Updated 2026-11-23 · 43 topic entries / 11 representative comparisons

Data and budget methods intervene at different points in training. Curricula reassess current difficulty, LESSER reduces selection-feature cost, STOPD randomly generates less and corrects estimates, BranchOPD adds important branches, Lightning caches teacher scores, and TAR retrieves suppressed correct modes. One fewer teacher call does not mean the entire run costs less.

[Mechanisms](#comparison) · [Trade-offs](#analysis) · [Cross-paper questions](#questions) · [Updates](#updates)

!!! note "How to read this card"

    The table compares representative methods. It is not a shared-benchmark leaderboard. Teaching examples are not measured results.

## Mechanism comparison {#comparison}

Axes: Selection unit: question, token position, suffix, or historical trajectory · Extra costs: difficulty estimation, forward features, teacher scoring, and bank construction · Statistical contracts: inverse-probability weights, independent branches under a fixed policy, and cache consistency · Student changes: difficulty reassessment, current log-probability refresh, and gates for suppressed modes

## Trade-off analysis {#analysis}

### Hard questions are not necessarily the most valuable for the current student

The curriculum uses current success rates, so an example can move into or out of a difficulty band after an update. LESSER approximates task-relevant gradient features rather than selecting by length or mistakes. Curriculum estimation costs rollouts, while LESSER needs candidate and target-query forwards. Compare total selection costs and never draw target queries from final test.

Sources: [A Step Harder, Not a Step Too Far: The Benefits and Limits of Curriculum Difficulty Progression in GRPO](../../../../reproductions/2610.13669-grpo-difficulty-curriculum/README-en.md) · [LESSER: Post-Training Data Selection with Output-Layer Gradients](../../../../post-training/2610.03702-lesser/README-en.md)

### Generation, scoring, and replay are different costs

STOPD randomly truncates before generation and corrects by retention probability. BranchOPD expands student suffixes at a fork without duplicating prefix credit. Lightning caches teacher scores; TAR caches verified base behavior and activates it according to current suppression. They add or remove different work, so neither training-step count nor teacher calls during training alone suffice.

Sources: [Does On-Policy Distillation Need to Complete Every Rollout?](../../../../post-training/2610.21337-stopd/README-en.md) · [Branching On-Policy Distillation](../../../../reproductions/2610.13481-branch-opd/README-en.md) · [Lightning OPD](../../../../post-training/2604.13010-lightning-opd/README-en.md) · [Preserving Reasoning Diversity in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards via Adaptive Replay](../../../../post-training/2610.24236-tar-adaptive-replay/README-en.md)

### Selection similarity must be interpreted for its own layer and purpose

LESSER's output-layer gradient features approximate relevance to target tasks. MAPLE's Hamming distance only compares categorical schema fields for donated initialization examples, including numeric bins treated as categories. Privacy comes from external AIM/PE accounting, not the selector; neither privacy nor generated-text quality follows from correct sorting.

Sources: [MAPLE: Metadata Augmented Private Language Evolution](../../../../post-training/2603.19258-maple-icl/README-en.md) · [LESSER: Post-Training Data Selection with Output-Layer Gradients](../../../../post-training/2610.03702-lesser/README-en.md)

### Why is inverse-probability debiasing absent?

SH-OPD retains the original token-mean objective and accepts systematic depth reweighting. Inverse-probability compensation belongs to its comparison STOPD, not this algorithm. GRPODropout filters completed rollouts by entropy contribution and does not save that round's generation. SH-OPD samples a shared cap before generation, changing depth exposure and actual budget. Existing Dropout checkpoint negative results also separate formula execution from capability gains. Local boundary: Power-survival distribution, one actual generation cap per batch, standard token-mean OPD and implicit position weights; no inverse-probability correction.

Sources: [Rethinking Supervision Scaling in On-Policy Distillation: From Dense Supervision to Stochastic Horizons](../../../../post-training/2611.20687-sh-opd/README-en.md) · [GRPODropout: Less is More for Online Reinforcement Learning Rollouts](../../../../post-training/2610.11854-grpo-dropout/README-en.md)

### Does migration simply copy the KV cache?

It uses stateless in-flight migration: the destination reconstructs state from prompt/generated tokens and resumes after one re-prefill, guarded by costs, reservations, hop limits and post-migration checks. GRPODropout filters responses after generation using entropy contribution and generally does not save generation. TailRoll may stop a tail response early and mask its partial loss, changing completed samples and system timing. Local boundary: Review actual multi-engine in-flight migration, one-time re-prefill and partial-output loss masking; no offline scheduler simulation claims system speedups.

Sources: [TAILROLL: Tail-Aware Rollout Acceleration for RL-Based LLM Post-Training](../../../../post-training/2611.22206-tailroll/README-en.md) · [GRPODropout: Less is More for Online Reinforcement Learning Rollouts](../../../../post-training/2610.11854-grpo-dropout/README-en.md)

### Why is bank size alone insufficient to compare CoLiR and TAR?

TAR builds a diverse bank of correct base-policy responses and applies suppression-gated weighted NLL to old trajectories and tokens. CoLiR selects historical prompts from cross-policy likelihood changes on initial incorrect and final correct responses, then generates fresh current-policy responses and applies KL only to replay. Both allocate historical replay budgets, but the units are stored behaviors versus historical questions, and the signals are current suppression versus improvement during the original task. Cost comparisons must separately include TAR bank construction, CoLiR cross-policy scoring and subsequent fresh rollouts. No extra generation for CoLiR memory construction does not mean generation-free training. Do not fill memory with all-correct/all-wrong final groups or all-correct initial groups. New-task and padding KL gradients must be zero. External training log likelihoods are inputs, not a fabricated scorer or agent success rate.

Sources: [Policy Improvement-Guided Replay for Continual Reinforcement Learning](../../../../post-training/2611.25989-colir-replay/README-en.md) · [Preserving Reasoning Diversity in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards via Adaptive Replay](../../../../post-training/2610.24236-tar-adaptive-replay/README-en.md)

### Can CTRL and CoLiR savings simply be multiplied?

CoLiR selects historical prompts and later regenerates responses with the current policy. CTRL controls hardware sharing and publication for training and generation. Data-budget/memory selection and system-layout/version contracts are separate axes. Reusing rollouts to build CoLiR memory does not remove later generation cost, so its savings cannot simply multiply CTRL's system speedups. Sources: Section3.3, Eq.1 and publication gate; Section3.4, Eq.3. b(y) is the earliest behavior version, including across resumed generation, not the completion version. Publication of g waits while requests dispatched at p satisfy g−p+1≥T; FIFO consumption with W≤T warmup closes the staleness bound. The lower bound on P guides measurement and SM-share selection. It does not guarantee attainability or permit a CPU scheduling sketch to establish throughput gains.

Sources: [CTRL: Concurrent Training and Rollout for LLM Reinforcement Learning via GPU Co-Residency](../../../../post-training/2611.27119-ctrl/README-en.md) · [Policy Improvement-Guided Replay for Continual Reinforcement Learning](../../../../post-training/2611.25989-colir-replay/README-en.md)

## Cross-paper questions {#questions}

Try answering before expanding the explanation. Each question relates at least two papers.

### If a curriculum finds a question too hard, should LESSER also discard it? {#cross-hardness-versus-selection-value}

??? note "Show answer and example"

    **Answer:** Not necessarily. A curriculum selects by current policy success, while LESSER applies its selection rule to candidate and target-query output gradients. A difficult example may share target knowledge or be beyond reach; difficulty alone does not determine gradient relevance. Both incur selection costs.

    **Illustrative example:** Teaching example: A domain question the student cannot yet solve may still share a target gradient direction. That neither guarantees value nor makes it zero.

    Sources: [A Step Harder, Not a Step Too Far: The Benefits and Limits of Curriculum Difficulty Progression in GRPO](../../../../reproductions/2610.13669-grpo-difficulty-curriculum/README-en.md) · [LESSER: Post-Training Data Selection with Output-Layer Gradients](../../../../post-training/2610.03702-lesser/README-en.md)

### STOPD and BranchOPD both change suffix budgets. Why not use the same early stop? {#cross-cutoff-versus-branch}

??? note "Show answer and example"

    **Answer:** STOPD randomly fixes a cutoff before generation and corrects retained tokens by inclusion probabilities. BranchOPD selects a fork and independently samples multiple continuations from the same frozen policy, counting the prefix once. One observes less and reweights; the other explores more at key states. Arbitrary post hoc truncation has neither contract.

    **Illustrative example:** Teaching example: Randomly stopping at token 64 and branching into three continuations at token 64 are opposite uses of budget.

    Sources: [Does On-Policy Distillation Need to Complete Every Rollout?](../../../../post-training/2610.21337-stopd/README-en.md) · [Branching On-Policy Distillation](../../../../reproductions/2610.13481-branch-opd/README-en.md)

### Why does TAR need current student probabilities while Lightning and TAR both reuse data? {#cross-teacher-cache-versus-behavior-bank}

??? note "Show answer and example"

    **Answer:** Lightning caches consistent teacher scores on initial student trajectories. TAR stores verified base behaviors and activates replay only where the current policy suppresses them relative to base, including token-level focus. A fixed bank does not fix weights, and zero teacher calls during training do not erase construction cost.

    **Illustrative example:** Teaching example: A base solution still produced frequently can get zero TAR replay even though cached teacher scores still exist.

    Sources: [Lightning OPD](../../../../post-training/2604.13010-lightning-opd/README-en.md) · [Preserving Reasoning Diversity in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards via Adaptive Replay](../../../../post-training/2610.24236-tar-adaptive-replay/README-en.md)

### Does metadata-nearest ICL selection reproduce private synthesis? {#cross-cross-colm-maple-icl}

??? note "Show answer and example"

    **Answer:** No. It is one initialization step; AIM, privacy accounting, the generator and AugPE are absent. The paper also finds initialization alone does not match full MAPLE.

    **Illustrative example:** Teaching example: choosing ten suitable public examples does not make later unprotected private voting safe.

    Sources: [MAPLE: Metadata Augmented Private Language Evolution](../../../../post-training/2603.19258-maple-icl/README-en.md) · [LESSER: Post-Training Data Selection with Output-Layer Gradients](../../../../post-training/2610.03702-lesser/README-en.md)

### Why not compare SH-OPD and GRPODropout only by retained sample count? {#cross-nov18-sh-opd}

??? note "Show answer and example"

    **Answer:** GRPODropout filters completed rollouts by entropy contribution and does not save that round's generation. SH-OPD samples a shared cap before generation, changing depth exposure and actual budget. Existing Dropout checkpoint negative results also separate formula execution from capability gains.

    **Illustrative example:** Teaching example: capping generation at four tokens differs from generating eight then filtering responses; generation costs require separate accounting.

    Sources: [Rethinking Supervision Scaling in On-Policy Distillation: From Dense Supervision to Stochastic Horizons](../../../../post-training/2611.20687-sh-opd/README-en.md) · [GRPODropout: Less is More for Online Reinforcement Learning Rollouts](../../../../post-training/2610.11854-grpo-dropout/README-en.md)

### How does this differ from GRPODropout? {#cross-nov18-tailroll}

??? note "Show answer and example"

    **Answer:** GRPODropout filters responses after generation using entropy contribution and generally does not save generation. TailRoll may stop a tail response early and mask its partial loss, changing completed samples and system timing.

    **Illustrative example:** Teaching example: a half-finished answer cannot be inserted as a completed incorrect sample while claiming an unchanged GRPO group.

    Sources: [TAILROLL: Tail-Aware Rollout Acceleration for RL-Based LLM Post-Training](../../../../post-training/2611.22206-tailroll/README-en.md) · [GRPODropout: Less is More for Online Reinforcement Learning Rollouts](../../../../post-training/2610.11854-grpo-dropout/README-en.md)

### Why is bank size alone insufficient to compare CoLiR and TAR? {#cross-nov20-colir-replay}

??? note "Show answer and example"

    **Answer:** CoLiR stores prompts and regenerates current-policy responses. TAR stores verified correct base-policy prototypes and gates old tokens by current suppression. Selection units, activation signals and generation costs differ;80 bank entries do not mean the same80 training trajectories.

    **Illustrative example:** Teaching example: two correct base solutions to one old question can have nonzero and zero TAR gates. If CoLiR retains the question, its next rollout may generate a third response.

    Sources: [Policy Improvement-Guided Replay for Continual Reinforcement Learning](../../../../post-training/2611.25989-colir-replay/README-en.md) · [Preserving Reasoning Diversity in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards via Adaptive Replay](../../../../post-training/2610.24236-tar-adaptive-replay/README-en.md)

### Can CTRL and CoLiR savings simply be multiplied? {#cross-nov23-ctrl}

??? note "Show answer and example"

    **Answer:** No. CoLiR chooses stored and replayed historical prompts; CTRL changes hardware layout and publication for training/generation. Costs and bottlenecks can overlap, requiring a real combined-system control absent here.

    **Illustrative example:** Teaching example: after removing a rollout batch, the learner may become the bottleneck, so an SM share tuned for long rollout may no longer be optimal.

    Sources: [CTRL: Concurrent Training and Rollout for LLM Reinforcement Learning via GPU Co-Residency](../../../../post-training/2611.27119-ctrl/README-en.md) · [Policy Improvement-Guided Replay for Continual Reinforcement Learning](../../../../post-training/2611.25989-colir-replay/README-en.md)
